# Implement block: Pull Lever Refresh (SwiftUI)

You are adding the "Pull Lever Refresh" block from Native Cook to the user's iOS app. The block already exists as working SwiftUI code. Your job is to bring it into this project faithfully, not to write a new one that looks similar.

## The block

A lever espresso machine drawn in Skia and shot like a product photo: one key light from the top left on a warm near-black studio sweep with a fine grain. A matte black body with a brushed steel top carries a 0–12 bar pressure gauge (polished bezel, printed scale, a brew zone from 8 to 10 bar, an orange needle under a domed glass) and a shot timer of two drums behind glass with a small amber pilot lamp. A polished chrome group head stands off it on a neck, with the lever on top (a brushed steel arm round a polished hub, a turned and lacquered walnut handle), the portafilter below (chrome basket, two spouts, walnut handle), and a white porcelain cup on the drip tray's slotted grate. Chrome, steel, walnut, porcelain, glass and coffee are SkSL runtime shaders that reflect one studio; the lever's highlights are computed from its angle, so its sheen and the walnut's lacquer move as it turns. Pump the lever down: each stroke adds 3 bar and the needle steps up with an overshoot ("Building pressure · 3 bar", "6 bar"); at 9 bar the brew zone lights ("Release to brew"). Let go and the spring pushes the lever back up slowly while the shot pours: first drips, then two thin tiger-striped streams that blond toward the end, the cup filling under a mottled hazelnut crema, the needle falling and the timer counting ("Brewing · 13 s"). When it is done the pilot lamp glows warm, steam rises and the copy reads "Espresso ready · 9 bar · 27 s · 36 g". Pull again and the full cup slides out while an empty one slides in. The machine is fitted with the lever's whole travel at least 16 pt inside both screen edges, under the copy.

**Motion.** Pan anywhere: a grab on the lever's side of the pivot turns it about the pivot with the finger (1:1 at the grab point); elsewhere the finger's travel down turns it as if it held the handle (0.42°/pt). The lever stands at −82° (screen angle, 0 is level to the right) and a stroke ends at −6°, with a rubber band past either stop (up to 5° above, 6° below, half after 40 pt). A stroke counts past −16° and re-arms above −58°: +3 bar, the needle springs to it (damping 12, stiffness 190, ζ ≈ 0.44), a 0.7 s vent of steam leaves the group, a rigid haptic. Let go between strokes and the lever springs back up (damping 26, stiffness 300, ζ ≈ 0.75) with the finger's angular velocity handed over. The third stroke reaches 9 bar: the brew zone lights over 360 ms and a medium haptic plays. Let go and the shot pours for 4.6 s (a time-lapse of 27 s): the lever rises on a bezier (0.25, 0.1, 0.25, 1), the needle falls to 1.4 bar on (0.45, 0, 0.6, 1), the flow drips until 17 % of the pour, runs steady, thins from 76 % and stops at 95 %, the cup fills and its crema forms, the timer drums step once a second (each turn over the last 22 % of the second). Done: a success haptic, the pilot lamp comes up over 700 ms, the needle settles to 0 over 900 ms, steam rises at 18 pt/s. A new pull swaps the cup: the full one slides 46 pt right and fades over 380 ms, an empty one slides back in over 460 ms (ease-out (0.23, 1, 0.32, 1)), and the timer blinks back to 00. Autoplay is a scripted finger on one 12 s loop: strokes at 0.7, 1.75 and 2.8 s (0.46 s down each), the third held to 4.0 s, the pour to 8.6 s, the ready beat, the cup swap at 10.6 s, back at rest by 11.5 s; a touch stops it and it resumes from rest 3.5 s after the last one. Reduce Motion: the needle and the lever's return are 180 ms fades instead of springs, the cup swaps in place with a cross-fade, the drums jump, and there is no steam, puff, ripple or wobble.

## Reference source

The block is built and running in the Native Cook source repository. Each link below is a file on GitHub. To read one as plain text, replace `https://github.com/Native-Cook/native-cook/blob/` with `https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Native-Cook/native-cook/` in its address.

### Demo (start here)

- [PullLeverRefreshDemo.swift](https://github.com/Native-Cook/native-cook/blob/main/swift/NativeCook/Blocks/Gestures/PullLeverRefresh/PullLeverRefreshDemo.swift)

### Files of the block

- [PullLeverRefresh.swift](https://github.com/Native-Cook/native-cook/blob/main/swift/NativeCook/Blocks/Gestures/PullLeverRefresh/PullLeverRefresh.swift)
- [PullLeverRefreshCaption.swift](https://github.com/Native-Cook/native-cook/blob/main/swift/NativeCook/Blocks/Gestures/PullLeverRefresh/PullLeverRefreshCaption.swift)
- [PullLeverRefreshModel.swift](https://github.com/Native-Cook/native-cook/blob/main/swift/NativeCook/Blocks/Gestures/PullLeverRefresh/PullLeverRefreshModel.swift)
- [PullLeverRefreshTokens.swift](https://github.com/Native-Cook/native-cook/blob/main/swift/NativeCook/Blocks/Gestures/PullLeverRefresh/PullLeverRefreshTokens.swift)
- [PullLeverRefreshTouchView.swift](https://github.com/Native-Cook/native-cook/blob/main/swift/NativeCook/Blocks/Gestures/PullLeverRefresh/PullLeverRefreshTouchView.swift)

### Frameworks

It needs no framework beyond SwiftUI.

## Your instructions

_Anything specific to this app goes here: where the block should appear, what to rename, what to change. Left empty, integrate the block as it is._

## How to work

Work like an experienced iOS engineer joining an existing project: learn the app first, read only what you need, decide early how the block fits, then integrate it with as little disruption as possible. Take the steps in order.

**Done means** the block is reachable in the user's app and behaves like the reference in the iOS Simulator or on a device. A SwiftUI preview is useful while you work, but it is not the proof: build and run the app.

**Fidelity.** Bring over the real implementation. Keep its structure, colours, sizes, timings and curves. Change only what this project requires and what "Your instructions" ask for.

If you already learned this project earlier in the conversation, reuse what you know and skip step 2. Learn it again only if the project changed or something you need is missing.

### 1. Check where you are

- You need the project's files and a terminal. If this prompt was pasted into a chat that has neither, stop and say so: it has to be run by a coding agent opened on the project.
- Confirm the project is an iOS app built with Xcode (an `.xcodeproj`, an `.xcworkspace` or a Swift package with an app target). If it is something else, stop, say what you found, and do not create a new app inside it unless the instructions ask for one.

### 2. Learn the host app

- The app target, its deployment target and its Swift version.
- SwiftUI, UIKit or both, and how a screen is shown today: `NavigationStack`, a coordinator, a tab bar, a storyboard.
- How files join the target: a folder the project synchronises, or a file list in the project that you have to extend.
- Conventions: folder layout, naming, where colours, fonts and assets live.
- Type names the app already uses, so the block's types do not collide with them.

### 3. Read the block

- Swift files in a module do not import each other, so the demo alone will not lead you to the rest. The list above names every file of the block: read them all.
- The demo is how the source repository shows the block. Bring over what the demo shows, not the repository's gallery. Anything listed under "Used by the demo only" stays behind.
- Read the block's initialiser and its defaults. The demo may switch on an option that makes the block play by itself for a recording (for example `autoPlay`). Keep the option; leave it off in the user's app unless asked.

### 4. Decide the fit

- The source app targets iOS 17. If the host targets an older system, check each API the block uses and tell the user what would have to change before you lower anything. Do not raise the host's deployment target without asking.
- If a type or function name of the block already exists in the app, rename the block's one, in every file that uses it, and say that you did.
- Shared helpers: copy the ones the block uses next to it, or fold them into the block's files. Do not copy helpers it never calls.
- In a UIKit app, show the block through a `UIHostingController`.

### 5. Bring it in

- Add the block's files to the app target, keeping their names.
- Copy its asset catalogs, loose resources and fonts, and check that the names the code asks for match the names in the bundle: a wrong name compiles and then shows nothing.
- A `.metal` file has to be compiled into the same target as the code that calls its function.
- Keep reduced-motion handling, haptics and accessibility labels as they are in the source.
- Mount the block where the instructions say. With no instructions, add a screen named after the block and make it reachable the way the app's other screens are.

### 6. Run it

- Build the app target for a simulator with `xcodebuild` or the project's own script, and fix every error and new warning the block introduced.
- Run it and use the block: every state, every gesture, light and dark appearance if the block follows them, and once with Reduce Motion on.
- If the build or the simulator fails for a reason outside the block, report the error and ask how to continue.

### 7. Report

- Files added and changed, and anything renamed to avoid a collision.
- How to reach the block in the app.
- Anything that differs from the reference, and why.
